title: Hickory vs Maple vs Oak Flooring: Durability, Janka Ratings and Price
meta: Hickory is hardest at 1,820 Janka, maple 1,450, oak 1,290 to 1,360. Wills Flooring compares durability, stain, stability and price for Sammamish family homes.
keywords: hickory vs maple vs oak flooring, Janka hardness hardwood flooring, hickory flooring pros and cons, maple hardwood floors dogs, best hardwood species for kids and dogs, Sammamish hardwood installation
offers: Hardwood floor installation, engineered or solid

blocks.lead: Hickory is the hardest of the three and the best at hiding damage, maple is hard but shows every scratch and stains badly, and oak is the balanced choice that takes stain well and hides wear, which is why it is still the default in Sammamish.
blocks.detail: Installation labor is the same for all three at Wills Flooring, $3.25 per sq ft for engineered or solid and $2.75 for unfinished. The species decides the material price, the look and how the floor ages with kids and dogs.

blocks.html: The typical Sammamish version of this question comes from a Klahanie or Trossachs family with two kids, a big dog and 1,200 sq ft of 1990s builder red oak on an open-plan main floor that has finally worn through. They want something that survives the next fifteen years, and someone told them hickory. Someone else said maple looks cleaner. Here is how the three hardwood species actually compare on the things that matter after the floor is in, not just in the sample box.

blocks.note: Janka ratings are industry standard tests of dent resistance and say nothing about scratch resistance, which depends on the finish. Material tiers are relative; the actual material price is quoted at the free estimate.

blocks.text: What Janka does and does not tell you

blocks.html: Janka measures the force needed to push a steel ball halfway into the wood. It predicts dents from dropped pans, chair legs and a 90 lb dog landing off the couch. It does not predict scratches, because scratches happen in the finish, not the wood, and all three species get the same finish. A maple floor at 1,450 shows more wear than a red oak at 1,290 in real houses because maple is pale and smooth, so every mark is visible, while oak's grain camouflages the same damage. Hardness matters; contrast and grain matter more for how a floor looks in year ten.

blocks.note: Labor is identical for hickory, maple and oak. The species you choose changes the material quote, which we bring with samples to the house.

items.title: Hickory
items.text: Nearly 40 percent harder than red oak, and the busy grain and color range from cream to dark brown hide scratches, dog nails and crumbs better than anything. The trade-offs: it moves a lot with humidity, so wide solid planks gap in winter, and staining evens the color at the cost of the character. Best as a wire-brushed or natural engineered plank in a busy Sammamish family house.

items.title: Hard maple
items.text: Pale, uniform and modern, the gym-floor wood. It is hard, but it is also the least forgiving floor of the three: scratches show as white lines, dents are obvious, and it takes stain unevenly, so dark maple often looks blotchy. It also moves with humidity. Choose it if you want the light Scandinavian look and are willing to keep it natural and refinish on schedule.

items.title: White and red oak
items.text: Oak is the compromise that keeps winning. Hard enough for dogs, stable enough for wide planks, and the only one of the three that stains evenly, so you can go light, gray, brown or dark. White oak is a touch harder and more neutral than red; red oak is the least expensive and matches most existing Sammamish builder floors if you are extending them.

blocks.text: Which one for a Sammamish house with kids and dogs?

a.title: Pick these when
items: Large dogs, a busy entry and an open plan where every room is a hallway
You want the floor to hide dents and scratches rather than avoid them
You prefer a natural or light finish with visible grain
You are replacing worn builder oak and want a clear upgrade

b.title: Think twice if
items: You want a dark or medium-brown stain
Dog nails and rolling toys are daily life
The house sits empty and cool for weeks; maple gaps and cups more than oak
You want the floor to look good between refinishes without much effort

blocks.text: A Pine Lake example with the math

blocks.html: A 1996 Pine Lake two-story: 1,200 sq ft of worn red oak on the main floor and 14 carpeted stairs to the bedrooms. Installing new engineered hickory or white oak: 1,200 × $3.25 + 14 × $125 = $3,900 + $1,750 = $5,650 in labor, plus the material, which is where the species shows up. The same job in red oak has identical labor and the lowest material line. If the existing oak were sound, refinishing it at $3.99 per sq ft would be the cheaper route, which is why we check the wood before quoting a replacement.

blocks.title: About wide planks:
blocks.text: Sammamish buyers want 7 in planks. Hickory and maple at that width in solid form gap noticeably every winter when the heat runs. If you want wide hickory or maple, choose engineered. Wide white oak is the most forgiving of the three in solid.
How to choose without regretting it

items.html: Look at large samples in your own light. Hickory's color range and maple's paleness read completely differently under a Sammamish gray sky than under showroom lights. Our mobile showroom brings full boards to the house for exactly this reason.
Decide on stain before species. If you want a dark or gray floor, you want oak. If you want the wood's own color, all three are open.
Drag a key across the samples. Do it. Then look at which one shows the line. That is your floor after one winter with a dog.
Match plank width to species. Narrow solid or wide engineered for hickory and maple; oak handles either.

Ask about the finish, not just the wood. A quality factory aluminum-oxide finish on prefinished planks, or three coats of Bona on a site-finished floor, does more for scratch resistance than 500 Janka points. Wills Flooring backs the installation with a 1-year workmanship warranty either way.

faq.q: Is hickory better than oak for flooring?
faq.a: For dent resistance and hiding damage, yes. Hickory rates 1,820 on the Janka scale against 1,290 to 1,360 for oak, and its varied grain camouflages scratches. Oak is more stable, stains far more evenly and costs less. For most Sammamish families, white oak is the better all-around choice; hickory wins in the hardest-used rooms.

Maple does not scratch more easily than oak, but every scratch shows. The wood is pale and smooth with almost no grain, so white scratch lines and dents stand out where oak or hickory would hide them. Households with dogs and kids usually find maple looks worn sooner even though it is technically harder.

faq.q: Can maple or hickory be stained dark?
faq.a: With difficulty. Maple's tight grain absorbs stain unevenly and often turns blotchy, especially in darker colors. Hickory takes stain but loses the color variation that makes it attractive. If you want a dark, gray or medium-brown floor, white oak stains most evenly and is the species we recommend for it.

faq.q: Does the species change the installation cost?
faq.a: Not the labor. Wills Flooring installs engineered or solid hardwood of any species at $3.25 per sq ft and unfinished hardwood at $2.75, with a 500 sq ft minimum and $125 per stair. The species changes the material price, which we quote with samples at the free in-home estimate.

faq.q: Which hardwood is most stable in the Pacific Northwest climate?
faq.a: White oak, followed by red oak. Hickory and maple both move more with humidity swings, which means wider seasonal gaps in winter when the heat runs. In a plateau home that stays heated and holds normal humidity all three work, but for wide solid planks white oak is the safest.

faq.q: What is the most durable hardwood floor for dogs?
faq.a: Hickory, for hardness and for hiding nail marks in its busy grain. White oak is a close second and easier to live with. Whatever the species, a matte or satin finish and a textured or wire-brushed surface hide dog wear better than a smooth, glossy floor, and nail trimming does more than any wood choice.
